# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison benefits those looking for a secure, self-hosted alternative to Slack, with a core use case of team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* **Cost**: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user per month.
* **Data Ownership**: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, while Slack's data ownership is subject to its terms of service.
* **Setup Complexity**: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to set up.
* **Scalability**: Slack is designed to scale with large teams, while Element's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities.
* **Feature Difference**: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for certain paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Has a user-friendly interface
* Limited control over data ownership
* Can be expensive for large teams
* Limited customization options
* Dependent on Slack's infrastructure
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and free
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* High level of customization and control
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Offers a high level of security and data ownership
* Can be complex to set up and maintain
* Limited user base and community compared to Slack
* Requires technical expertise to self-host

## When to Choose Each
When to choose Slack: Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and have a large budget. It's also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the Slack ecosystem and have many integrations set up. However, for teams that value data ownership and security, Slack may not be the best choice.
When to choose Element: Element is a good choice for teams that value data ownership and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution. It's also a good choice for teams that are looking for a free or low-cost alternative to Slack, and are comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting.

## Migration Path

2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires a high level of technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities, which can be a challenge for large teams. However, for teams that value data ownership and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution, Element is a good choice.

## Who Should Switch

* Teams that value data ownership and security above all else.

* Teams that are comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting.
